title: The Teacher Who Refused to Make It Easy
script: Narrator: [nostalgic] Mrs. Herrera was, by any conventional metric, an unpopular teacher, the kind students traded warnings about before ever setting foot in her classroom.
Narrator: [thoughtful] She returned essays covered in a shade of red ink so dense it looked less like feedback than an indictment, and she refused, categorically, to round a grade up out of sympathy.
Narrator: [honest] I resented her thoroughly for most of that year, convinced she simply enjoyed watching seventeen-year-olds squirm under the weight of her impossible standards.

Narrator: [reflective] It wasn't until years later, drafting a report at my first real job, that I noticed my own internal editor sounded suspiciously like her, dismantling a weak argument before anyone else had the chance to.
Narrator: [wry] I'd absorbed, apparently without consenting to it, an entire framework for interrogating my own thinking that no amount of gentler feedback had ever managed to install.

Narrator: [with feeling] What I hadn't understood as a teenager was that her severity wasn't indifference; it was a kind of respect, an assumption that we were capable of more than we were currently producing.
Narrator: [candid] The teachers who praised everything indiscriminately, by contrast, left me with a vague, untested confidence that dissolved the moment it met any real resistance.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I've since tried to write her a letter twice, and abandoned it twice, uncertain how to convey gratitude for something that felt, at the time, indistinguishable from cruelty.
Narrator: [determined] I think what I'd actually say, if I ever finish the letter, is that she taught me the difference between being comforted and being taken seriously.
Narrator: [warmly] And that the second one, however unpleasant it felt at seventeen, turned out to matter considerably more in the long run.
